options.feedback: Iron sulfide is a genuine chemical compound with new, distinct properties -- it's fundamentally different from the original simple physical mixture.

hints.hard: The property of magnetism belongs specifically to free iron atoms/crystals -- once chemically bonded into a new compound, that original property is superseded by the compound's own distinct characteristics.
hints.medium: Once the iron chemically combines with sulfur to form something new, it's not "free" iron anymore, so its magnetic property is gone.
hints.easy: Once the iron combines with sulfur to make something new, it's not really "iron" anymore in the way a magnet would recognize.

questions.text: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?

options.text: To show that atoms are neither created nor destroyed during the reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- balancing reflects the fundamental law of conservation of mass at the atomic level.

options.text: To make the equation look neater
options.feedback: Balancing isn't about appearance -- it's about accurately representing the conservation of matter.

options.text: To make the reaction happen faster
options.feedback: Balancing an equation on paper doesn't affect the actual reaction speed -- that's influenced by factors like temperature and catalysts.

options.text: It isn't actually necessary for most reactions
options.feedback: Balancing is a required, fundamental step for accurately representing any real chemical reaction.

hints.hard: This principle ensures that matter is conserved throughout a chemical transformation.
hints.medium: This ensures no atoms mysteriously appear or disappear during the reaction.
hints.easy: This makes sure no atoms just disappear or appear out of nowhere.

questions.text: In the unbalanced equation Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃, why is this equation not yet balanced?

options.text: The number of iron and oxygen atoms differs between the reactant and product sides
options.feedback: Correct -- counting atoms on each side reveals a mismatch, meaning coefficients are needed to balance it.

options.text: The equation actually is already perfectly balanced
options.feedback: Counting atoms carefully shows this equation is NOT balanced as written -- coefficients are needed.

options.text: Iron and oxygen can't react with each other at all
options.feedback: Iron and oxygen do react (forming rust, Fe₂O₃) -- the issue here is specifically about balancing atom counts, not whether they can react.

options.text: The equation has too many arrows
options.feedback: There's only one arrow here, which is standard -- the actual issue is with atom counts on each side, not the number of arrows.

hints.hard: Count each type of atom present on the reactant side and compare it to the count on the product side.
hints.medium: Count the iron atoms and oxygen atoms on each side separately and compare them.
hints.easy: Count the iron atoms and oxygen atoms on each side -- they don't match yet.

questions.text: When balancing a chemical equation, why are you only allowed to change the coefficients (numbers in front of formulas) and never the subscripts (numbers within a formula)?

options.text: Changing a subscript would alter the actual chemical identity of the substance, creating a completely different compound rather than just adjusting quantity
options.feedback: Correct -- coefficients scale the QUANTITY of a substance, while subscripts define the substance's fundamental composition/identity.

options.text: Changing subscripts is actually allowed and commonly done when balancing
options.feedback: Changing subscripts is NOT allowed in proper balancing -- doing so would incorrectly change the identity of the substance itself.

options.text: Coefficients and subscripts mean exactly the same thing
options.feedback: These are fundamentally different -- coefficients indicate quantity of molecules, while subscripts indicate atom composition within a single molecule.

options.text: There is no actual rule about this in chemistry
options.feedback: This is actually a fundamental, strictly enforced rule in properly balancing chemical equations.

hints.hard: Subscripts are fixed by the actual bonding structure and identity of a specific compound, while coefficients simply indicate how many separate molecules of that unchanged compound are present.
hints.medium: Changing a subscript would actually turn the substance into a completely different chemical, not just change how much of it there is.
hints.easy: Changing a subscript would turn the substance into a totally different chemical, not just more or less of the same one.

questions.text: If two objects have the same volume but different masses, which one has greater density?

options.text: The one with greater mass
options.feedback: Correct -- since density = mass/volume, and volume is the same for both, more mass means higher density.

options.text: The one with less mass
options.feedback: This is backwards -- with equal volume, MORE mass means higher density, not less.

options.text: They must have equal density, since their volumes are equal
options.feedback: Equal volume doesn't guarantee equal density if their masses are different -- density depends on both mass and volume together.

options.text: Density cannot be determined from mass and volume
options.feedback: Density is defined specifically as mass divided by volume -- it absolutely can be determined from these two values.

hints.hard: Density scales directly with the amount of mass packed into a given, fixed volume.
hints.medium: With the same amount of space, having more "stuff" packed in means higher density.
hints.easy: With the same size, having more mass packed in means it's more dense.

questions.text: A scientist finds an unknown metal sample with a mass of 39 grams and a volume of 5 cm³. Referencing known densities (aluminum ≈2.7 g/cm³, iron ≈7.9 g/cm³, gold ≈19.3 g/cm³), which metal does this sample most likely match?

options.text: Iron, since the sample's density (39÷5=7.8 g/cm³) is very close to iron's known density
options.feedback: Correct -- comparing calculated density to known reference values is a standard way to help identify an unknown substance.

options.text: Aluminum, since the sample is a metal
options.feedback: Simply being a metal doesn't determine which specific metal it is -- the calculated density (7.8 g/cm³) is far closer to iron's than aluminum's.

options.text: Gold, since gold is a well-known metal
options.feedback: Being well-known isn't relevant -- the calculated density (7.8 g/cm³) is far closer to iron's density than gold's much higher density.

options.text: It's impossible to identify the metal from this information
options.feedback: Mass and volume are exactly the information needed to calculate density and compare it against known reference values.

hints.hard: Divide the sample's mass by its volume, then compare the result to the known density values for each candidate metal.
hints.medium: Divide 39 by 5 to find the sample's density, then compare it to the listed known densities.
hints.easy: Divide 39 by 5 to get 7.8, then see which metal's density that's closest to.

questions.text: Two samples of the same pure substance, one large and one small, are compared. What would you expect to be true about their densities, and why?

options.text: Their densities should be equal, because density is an intensive property that doesn't depend on the amount of substance present
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike mass or volume alone (extensive properties), density remains constant for a given pure substance regardless of sample size.

options.text: The larger sample will always have a higher density
options.feedback: Density doesn't scale with sample size for the same pure substance -- it should remain constant.

options.text: The smaller sample will always have a higher density
options.feedback: Density doesn't scale with sample size for the same pure substance -- it should remain constant, not favor the smaller piece.

options.text: Density cannot be compared between samples of different sizes
options.feedback: Density is precisely a property designed to allow meaningful comparison between samples of ANY size, since it's normalized per unit volume.

hints.hard: As an intensive property, density is defined per unit volume/mass and is therefore independent of the total quantity of a pure, uniform substance present.
hints.medium: Since it's the exact same substance, doubling or halving the amount doesn't change how tightly packed its mass is for any given size.
hints.easy: Since it's the same substance, a bigger or smaller piece should still weigh the same amount for its size.

questions.text: What is a pure substance?

options.text: Matter with a fixed, uniform composition throughout -- either a single element or compound
options.feedback: Correct -- pure substances have consistent properties throughout, unlike mixtures.

options.text: Any matter that looks clean and clear
options.feedback: Visual clarity isn't the scientific definition -- a pure substance is defined by having a fixed, uniform composition.

options.text: A combination of two or more different substances
options.feedback: That describes a mixture, the opposite of a pure substance.

options.text: Only substances found in nature, never made in a lab
options.feedback: Pure substances can be either natural or artificially created -- the origin doesn't determine purity in this chemical sense.

hints.hard: This category of matter maintains one consistent chemical identity throughout, unlike a blended combination.
hints.medium: This is matter with the exact same makeup all the way through, not a blend of different things.
hints.easy: This is matter that's just one single thing all the way through, not a blend.

questions.text: Which of the following is a pure substance, rather than a mixture?

options.text: Distilled water (H₂O only)

options.text: Ocean water

options.text: Soil

options.text: Orange juice
options.feedback: Orange juice contains water, sugars, pulp, and other components, making it a mixture, not a pure substance.

hints.hard: Look for the option where all other dissolved or suspended substances have been removed, leaving only one chemical compound.
hints.medium: Look for the option where nothing else has been added or dissolved into it.
hints.easy: Distilled water has had everything else removed, leaving just water itself.

questions.text: Air is often used as an everyday example of matter, but chemically speaking, why is it classified as a mixture rather than a pure substance?

options.text: Air is actually a pure substance made of just one gas

options.text: Air doesn't contain any matter at all
options.feedback: Air is absolutely made of matter -- specifically, a mixture of various gas molecules.

options.text: Air's composition is exactly identical everywhere on Earth at all times
options.feedback: Air's exact composition can actually vary somewhat (e.g., humidity, altitude, pollution levels), which is consistent with it being a mixture, not a fixed pure substance.

hints.hard: Since air's components (various gas molecules) are not chemically bonded together and their relative amounts can vary somewhat, it satisfies the definition of a mixture rather than a fixed-composition pure substance.
hints.medium: Air is made of a bunch of different gases just floating together, not chemically stuck together, and the exact mix can vary a bit.
hints.easy: Air is made of different gases mixed together, not chemically stuck together as one single substance.

questions.text: The rule 'like dissolves like' suggests that polar solvents (like water) tend to dissolve what kind of solutes best?

options.text: Other polar substances
options.feedback: Correct -- polar solvents generally dissolve other polar or ionic substances well.

options.text: Only nonpolar substances
options.feedback: Nonpolar substances generally dissolve poorly in polar solvents like water -- that's the opposite of this rule.

options.text: Only metals in solid form

options.text: Nothing at all -- polar solvents dissolve nothing
options.feedback: Polar solvents like water are actually excellent at dissolving many substances, particularly other polar or ionic ones.

hints.easy: Similar types of substances tend to mix well together.

questions.text: Oil (nonpolar) doesn't mix well with water (polar). What does this demonstrate about the 'like dissolves like' principle?

options.text: Substances with different polarities (one polar, one nonpolar) tend to not mix or dissolve well together
options.feedback: Correct -- this mismatch in polarity is exactly why oil and water famously separate rather than mix.

options.text: Oil and water should actually mix perfectly according to this rule

options.text: This principle doesn't apply to liquids at all

options.text: Oil has no polarity classification at all

hints.easy: Since oil and water are different types (nonpolar vs polar), think about whether they'd mix well.

questions.text: Soap can help mix oil and water together because soap molecules have both a polar (hydrophilic) end and a nonpolar (hydrophobic) end. How does this dual structure allow soap to bridge the two substances?

options.text: The nonpolar end of soap molecules surrounds oil droplets while the polar end interacts with water, effectively linking the two otherwise incompatible substances together
options.feedback: Correct -- this dual-affinity structure is exactly what allows soap to act as an emulsifier, letting oil and water mix in a stable way.

options.text: Soap actually removes all polarity from both oil and water
options.feedback: Soap doesn't eliminate polarity from either substance -- its own dual-ended structure is what bridges the two, not by altering their inherent properties.

options.text: Soap molecules are entirely nonpolar, just like oil
options.feedback: Soap molecules specifically have BOTH a polar and a nonpolar end -- that dual nature is exactly what gives it its bridging ability.

options.text: This has nothing to do with polarity at all
options.feedback: This effect is entirely explained by soap's dual-polarity molecular structure, directly relevant to the like-dissolves-like principle.

hints.hard: Soap's amphiphilic structure (having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions) lets one end associate with each of the two otherwise-incompatible substances, forming a stable connecting bridge.
hints.medium: One end of the soap molecule likes to stick to oil, and the other end likes to stick to water, connecting the two together.
hints.easy: One end of the soap molecule sticks to oil, and the other end sticks to water, connecting the two.

questions.text: What generally happens to a gas when it is compressed under increasing pressure at a constant temperature?

options.text: It can turn into a liquid if compressed enough
options.feedback: Correct -- sufficient pressure can force gas molecules close enough together to become a liquid.

options.text: It always stays a gas no matter how much pressure is applied
options.feedback: With enough pressure, most gases can actually be forced into a liquid state.

options.text: It immediately turns into a solid

options.text: It disappears completely

hints.easy: Squeezing a gas hard enough can turn it into a liquid.

questions.text: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitudes (like on a mountain) compared to sea level. Why does this happen?

options.text: Lower atmospheric pressure at high altitude means less pressure needs to be overcome for water molecules to escape into vapor, so boiling occurs at a lower temperature

options.text: Mountains are always colder, which somehow makes water boil at a lower temperature

options.text: Water at high altitude is a completely different chemical substance

options.text: This is a myth, and boiling point doesn't actually change with altitude

hints.hard: The surrounding pressure directly determines how much energy is needed for molecules to escape the liquid's surface into vapor form.

questions.text: A substance's phase diagram shows the specific combinations of temperature and pressure at which it exists as a solid, liquid, or gas. Why is a single temperature value (like '100°C for boiling') actually an oversimplification?

options.text: The boiling point (and other phase transition points) actually depends on both temperature AND pressure together, not temperature alone
options.feedback: Correct -- the commonly cited '100°C' boiling point specifically assumes standard atmospheric pressure; changing pressure shifts that boiling point.

options.text: Temperature has no actual effect on phase transitions
options.feedback: Temperature absolutely does affect phase transitions -- but so does pressure, which is exactly the point being made here.

options.text: All substances actually boil at exactly the same temperature, regardless of pressure
options.feedback: Different substances have different boiling points, AND for any given substance, that boiling point changes with pressure.

options.text: Phase diagrams are purely theoretical and don't reflect real-world behavior
options.feedback: Phase diagrams accurately reflect real, measurable, and highly practical phase-transition behavior of substances under different conditions.

hints.hard: Phase transition points are defined by a specific temperature-pressure PAIR, not temperature in isolation -- a commonly cited value like 100°C implicitly assumes one specific, standard pressure.
hints.medium: The temperature where something boils actually changes depending on the surrounding pressure, so quoting just one temperature leaves out important information.
hints.easy: The temperature where water boils actually changes depending on the pressure around it, like on a mountain.

questions.text: Which type of compound generally has a higher melting point: ionic or molecular (covalent)?

options.text: Molecular (covalent) compounds
options.feedback: Molecular compounds generally have weaker intermolecular forces, resulting in LOWER melting points compared to ionic compounds.

options.text: They always have exactly the same melting point
options.feedback: There's a general, well-documented difference in typical melting points between these two compound categories.

options.text: Neither type of compound has a melting point
options.feedback: Both ionic and molecular compounds do have defined melting points -- they just tend to differ significantly in value.

hints.hard: This bonding type creates an extensive network of strong, uniform electrostatic attractions throughout the solid structure.

questions.text: Ionic compounds like table salt conduct electricity when dissolved in water or melted, but not in their solid form. Why?

options.text: In the solid state, ions are locked in a fixed lattice and can't move freely, but when dissolved or melted, they become mobile and can carry electric charge
options.feedback: Correct -- electrical conductivity in ionic compounds specifically requires the ions to be free to move, which only happens outside the rigid solid structure.

options.text: Solid ionic compounds don't actually contain any charged particles
options.feedback: Solid ionic compounds definitely contain charged ions -- they're just locked in place within a rigid structure, unable to move and carry current.

options.text: Ionic compounds can never conduct electricity under any circumstances
options.feedback: Ionic compounds CAN conduct electricity, specifically when dissolved in water or melted, allowing their ions to move freely.

options.text: This has nothing to do with the movement of charged particles
options.feedback: This phenomenon is entirely explained by whether the charged ions are free to move (conducting) or locked in place (non-conducting).

hints.hard: Conductivity requires charged particles free to migrate through the material -- a condition met only when the rigid ionic lattice is disrupted (melting or dissolving).
hints.medium: The charged particles need to be free to move around in order to carry electricity, which only happens once the solid structure breaks down.
hints.easy: The charged particles need to be free to move around to carry electricity, which only happens once melted or dissolved.

questions.text: Why are molecular (covalent) compounds generally poor conductors of electricity, even when dissolved in water or melted, unlike ionic compounds?

options.feedback: Correct -- without charged, mobile ions (or free electrons), there's no effective way for these compounds to carry an electric current.

options.text: Molecular compounds actually conduct electricity better than ionic compounds in every situation
options.feedback: This is generally backwards -- ionic compounds (when dissolved/melted) typically conduct electricity much better than molecular compounds.

options.text: Molecular compounds don't actually contain any atoms
options.feedback: Molecular compounds are definitely made of atoms, just held together by shared electrons (covalent bonds) rather than forming free-moving charged ions.

options.text: Electricity requires heat, which molecular compounds cannot produce
options.feedback: Electrical conductivity is about the presence of mobile charged particles, not about a substance's ability to produce heat.

hints.hard: Since covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs rather than distinct, mobile charged ions, molecular compounds generally lack the free charge carriers necessary for electrical conductivity, regardless of physical state.
hints.medium: Since these compounds are made of neutral molecules without loose charged particles, there's nothing available to actually carry an electric current.
hints.easy: Since these compounds don't have loose charged particles, there's nothing there to actually carry electricity.

questions.text: In terms of electrons, what happens during oxidation?

questions.text: Oxidation and reduction always occur together in a single reaction (called a redox reaction), never in isolation. Why must this always be the case?

options.text: This pairing is just a naming coincidence with no real chemical basis

options.text: Reduction reactions can happen without any electrons being involved at all

questions.text: Which observation is the strongest evidence that a chemical change has occurred?

questions.text: On the pH scale, a value of 7 is considered:

questions.text: Which subatomic particle has a positive charge?

questions.text: Where are electrons located relative to the nucleus of an atom?

questions.text: An atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons, and 6 electrons. If it gains 2 extra electrons, what does it become?

questions.text: In a balanced chemical equation, what must be equal on both sides?

options.text: The number of atoms of each element

questions.text: To balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, what coefficients are needed?

options.text: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
options.feedback: Correct -- this gives 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on both sides.

options.text: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O

options.text: H₂ + 2O₂ → H₂O

hints.hard: Start by balancing hydrogen atoms using a coefficient, then check whether oxygen atoms also balance afterward.

questions.text: When balancing CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, what is the correct set of coefficients?

options.text: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
options.feedback: Correct -- this balances 1 C, 4 H, and 4 O on both sides.

options.text: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
options.feedback: As written, oxygen and hydrogen atoms don't balance between the two sides.

options.text: 2CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

options.text: CH₄ + 2O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O

hints.hard: Balance carbon first, then hydrogen using water's coefficient, then count total oxygen needed on the right to determine oxygen gas's coefficient last.
hints.medium: Balance carbon and hydrogen first using the product coefficients, then figure out how much oxygen gas is needed to match.
hints.easy: Balance the carbons and hydrogens first, then adjust the oxygen gas amount to match what's needed.

questions.text: What happens to electrons in an ionic bond?

questions.text: Which type of bond typically forms between two nonmetal atoms?

hints.easy: When two nonmetals bond, they usually share their electrons instead of one stealing from the other.

questions.text: Why do ionic compounds generally have higher melting points than covalent compounds?

options.text: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions requires more energy to break

options.text: Ionic compounds are always heavier

options.text: Covalent compounds contain more atoms
options.feedback: Atom count doesn't determine bond strength or melting point in this way.

options.text: Ionic compounds don't actually have a fixed melting point
options.feedback: Ionic compounds do have well-defined, typically high, melting points.

hints.hard: The lattice structure formed by oppositely charged ions creates very strong, uniform attractive forces throughout the solid, unlike the more localized bonds in covalent molecules.

hints.easy: Ionic compounds hold together very tightly because of strong attraction between oppositely charged particles.

questions.text: In a solution of salt water, what is the salt called?

options.text: The solute

options.text: The precipitate

questions.text: If you add more solute to a fixed amount of solvent, what happens to the solution's concentration?

questions.text: A solution is described as 'saturated.' What does this mean?

options.text: It contains no solute at all

options.text: It has reached its boiling point
options.feedback: Saturation is about how much solute is dissolved, not about temperature or boiling.

options.text: It is chemically unstable and about to react

questions.text: According to the law of conservation of mass, what happens to mass during a chemical reaction?

questions.text: A sealed container holds a burning candle. Why does the total mass inside the sealed container stay the same, even though the candle appears to shrink?

questions.text: Which of the following is a pure element?

questions.text: What does VSEPR theory help predict about a molecule?

questions.text: According to VSEPR theory, why do electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible?

options.text: Because electron pairs repel each other (like charges), so they naturally position themselves to minimize this repulsion

options.text: Because electron pairs are strongly attracted to each other

options.text: Because the central atom pushes them into a random arrangement
options.feedback: The arrangement isn't random -- it specifically minimizes repulsion between the negatively charged electron pairs.

options.text: Hydrogen atoms always repel each other strongly, regardless of the central atom

options.text: Molecule
options.feedback: A molecule is made of two or more atoms bonded together, not the smallest single unit.

options.text: Cell
options.feedback: A cell is a biological unit, unrelated to the smallest unit of a chemical element.

options.text: Compound
options.feedback: A compound is made of different elements bonded together, larger than a single atom.

hints.hard: This is the fundamental unit that keeps an element's identity, before any bonding occurs.
hints.medium: This is the basic particle that makes up all matter, retaining the identity of its element.
hints.easy: This is the tiny basic building block that makes up all elements.

questions.text: What is a molecule?

options.text: Two or more atoms bonded together
options.feedback: Correct -- molecules form when atoms join through chemical bonds.

options.text: A single, unbonded atom
options.feedback: A single atom alone isn't considered a molecule.

options.text: A mixture of unrelated substances
options.feedback: A mixture involves substances that aren't chemically bonded, unlike a molecule.

options.text: The nucleus of an atom
options.feedback: The nucleus is a component inside a single atom, not a combination of atoms.

hints.hard: This structure forms specifically when individual atoms link together through shared or transferred electrons.
hints.medium: This forms when two or more atoms join together through a chemical bond.
hints.easy: This is what you get when atoms join together.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes an O₂ molecule versus a single O atom?

options.text: O₂ is two oxygen atoms chemically bonded together, while a single O atom exists alone
options.feedback: Correct -- O₂ is the stable diatomic form oxygen naturally exists as, made of two bonded atoms.

options.text: O₂ and a single O atom are exactly the same thing, just written differently
options.feedback: They're chemically distinct -- one is a bonded pair, the other is a standalone atom.

options.text: O₂ has twice the number of protons as a single O atom
options.feedback: O₂ has two separate oxygen atoms bonded together, not one atom with double the protons.

options.text: O₂ is a compound, while a single O atom is a mixture
options.feedback: O₂ is a molecule of a single element (not a compound, which requires different elements), and a lone atom isn't a mixture.

hints.hard: Focus on the bonding relationship: O₂ represents two identical atoms joined by a covalent bond, distinct from either an isolated atom or a compound of different elements.
hints.medium: O₂ is two oxygen atoms bonded together as the same element, not a different substance entirely.
hints.easy: O₂ is just two oxygen atoms stuck together, while a lone O atom is by itself.

questions.text: What are valence electrons?

options.text: The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom
options.feedback: Correct -- valence electrons occupy the outermost energy level and determine bonding behavior.

options.text: The electrons closest to the nucleus
options.feedback: Electrons closest to the nucleus are inner-shell electrons, not valence electrons.

options.text: All the protons in an atom
options.feedback: Protons are a completely different particle, located in the nucleus, not valence electrons at all.

options.text: The neutrons that hold the nucleus together
options.feedback: Neutrons are nuclear particles, unrelated to valence electrons.

hints.hard: These are the electrons positioned in the shell furthest from the atom's center.
hints.medium: These electrons sit in the outermost energy level of the atom.
hints.easy: These are the electrons in the outside layer of an atom.

questions.text: Why do atoms tend to form bonds with other atoms?

options.text: To achieve a more stable arrangement of valence electrons, often a full outer shell
options.feedback: Correct -- atoms bond to reach a lower-energy, more stable electron configuration.

options.text: To increase the total number of protons they have
options.feedback: Bonding doesn't change the number of protons in an atom -- that would change the element itself.

options.text: To become radioactive
options.feedback: Radioactivity relates to unstable nuclei, not the general reason atoms form chemical bonds.

options.text: To lose all of their electrons entirely
options.feedback: Atoms seek stability, which usually means gaining, losing, or sharing just a few electrons -- not losing all of them.

hints.hard: Atoms bond in order to reach the lowest-energy, most stable configuration of electrons, typically a full outer shell.
hints.medium: Bonding helps atoms fill up their outer electron shell to become more stable.
hints.easy: Atoms bond to try to fill up their outer shell of electrons.

questions.text: An atom has 7 valence electrons. Based on the octet rule, what is it most likely to do when bonding?

options.text: Gain 1 electron to complete a stable set of 8
options.feedback: Correct -- gaining just 1 electron is the shortest path to a full, stable outer shell of 8.

options.text: Lose 7 electrons to have none left
options.feedback: Losing all 7 electrons is far less favorable than simply gaining 1 to complete the octet.

options.text: Gain 5 more electrons
options.feedback: This overshoots the stable octet of 8 valence electrons.

options.text: Do nothing, since 7 is already a stable number
options.feedback: 7 valence electrons is not a stable configuration -- 8 is the stable target under the octet rule.

hints.hard: Compare the effort of gaining 1 electron versus losing 7 -- the smaller change toward a full octet is always the energetically favorable path.
hints.medium: It's much easier for the atom to gain just 1 electron than to lose all 7 to reach a stable configuration.
hints.easy: Gaining just 1 more electron gets this atom to a stable total of 8 -- that's the easier path.

questions.text: What makes two atoms of the same element isotopes of each other?

options.text: They have different numbers of neutrons
options.feedback: Correct -- isotopes share the same number of protons but differ in neutron count.

options.text: They have different numbers of protons
options.feedback: Different proton counts would make them different elements entirely, not isotopes.

options.text: They have different numbers of electrons only, with the same protons and neutrons
options.feedback: That describes an ion, not an isotope.

options.text: They are found in different countries
options.feedback: Geographic location has no bearing on what defines an isotope.

hints.hard: This particle's count in the nucleus can vary between isotopes without changing the identity of the element.
hints.medium: This is the particle in the nucleus that has no electric charge, and its count can vary between isotopes.
hints.easy: The number of these neutral particles in the nucleus differs between isotopes.

questions.text: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. What do the numbers 12 and 14 represent?

options.text: The mass number (protons + neutrons)
options.feedback: Correct -- the number after the element name is the total mass number.

options.text: The number of protons only
options.feedback: Both isotopes have the same number of protons (6) -- the numbers reflect total mass, not proton count alone.

options.text: The number of electrons only
options.feedback: Electron count isn't what distinguishes these two isotopes -- neutron count is.

options.text: The atomic charge
options.feedback: These numbers describe mass, not electrical charge.

hints.hard: This number combines two types of nuclear particles into a single total.
hints.medium: This number adds together the protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
hints.easy: This number is the total count of protons and neutrons combined.

questions.text: Carbon-14 has 6 protons and a mass number of 14. How many neutrons does it have?

options.feedback: Correct -- mass number minus protons: 14-6=8 neutrons.
This assumes protons and neutrons are always equal, which isn't true for this isotope.
This uses the mass number directly instead of subtracting the proton count.
This adds protons and mass number instead of subtracting.

hints.hard: Subtract the atomic number (proton count) from the mass number to isolate the neutron count.
hints.medium: Subtract the number of protons from the mass number to find the neutrons.
hints.easy: Subtract 6 from 14 to find the number of neutrons.

questions.text: What is the general purpose of a universal indicator?

options.text: To show a range of colors corresponding to different pH levels
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike single-color indicators, a universal indicator shows a whole spectrum of colors across the pH scale.

options.text: To measure the temperature of a solution
options.feedback: A universal indicator measures pH (acidity/basicity), not temperature.

options.text: To measure the exact mass of a solution
options.feedback: Mass measurement isn't the purpose of a pH indicator -- it's specifically about showing acidity/basicity via color.

options.text: To make a solution taste different
options.feedback: Indicators are visual tools showing color change, not something that affects taste.

hints.hard: This tool visually reveals a solution's approximate position along the full acid-to-base spectrum.
hints.medium: This tool shows a whole range of colors depending on how acidic or basic something is.
hints.easy: This tool changes into different colors depending on how acidic or basic something is.

questions.text: A universal indicator turns red in one solution and dark blue/purple in another. What does this suggest about the two solutions?

options.text: The red solution is strongly acidic, while the dark blue/purple solution is strongly basic
options.feedback: Correct -- universal indicators typically show red for strong acids and blue/purple for strong bases, with green representing neutral.

options.text: Both solutions have exactly the same pH
options.feedback: Different colors specifically indicate DIFFERENT pH levels -- if they had the same pH, the indicator would show the same color for both.

options.text: The red solution is basic, and the blue solution is acidic
options.feedback: This is backwards for a standard universal indicator -- red typically signals acidic, and blue/purple typically signals basic.

options.text: This color difference has nothing to do with pH
options.feedback: This color difference is specifically and directly tied to the pH difference between the two solutions.

hints.hard: Recall the typical color-coding convention: warm colors (red/orange) for acidic, cool colors (blue/purple) for basic, with green in the middle for neutral.
hints.medium: Remember that red typically signals strong acid, and blue/purple typically signals strong base on this type of indicator.
hints.easy: Red usually means acidic, and blue/purple usually means basic.

questions.text: Different indicators (like litmus, phenolphthalein, and universal indicator) change color at different, specific pH ranges. Why might a chemist choose a specific indicator rather than always using a universal indicator?

options.text: A specific indicator with a narrow, well-defined color-change range can more precisely pinpoint whether a solution has crossed a particular pH threshold relevant to their experiment
options.feedback: Correct -- for identifying a precise endpoint (like in a titration), a sharp, specific color change at a known pH is often more useful than a broad, gradual color spectrum.

options.text: There is no real reason -- all indicators work identically in every situation
options.feedback: Different indicators actually have genuinely different, useful properties (specific color-change pH ranges) suited to different experimental needs.

options.text: Specific indicators are always cheaper than universal indicators, which is the only reason for choosing them
options.feedback: While cost might be A factor, the PRIMARY scientific reason for choosing a specific indicator relates to its precise, well-defined pH transition range, not simply cost.

options.text: Specific indicators can only be used with acids, never with bases
options.feedback: Specific indicators can be selected for use across various points along the pH scale, working with both acid-related and base-related transitions depending on the indicator chosen.

hints.hard: A narrow-range indicator provides a sharp, unambiguous color change precisely at a known pH value, which is more useful for detecting a specific threshold than a gradual, broad-spectrum color shift.
hints.medium: A specific indicator gives a sharp, clear color change right at one particular pH point, which is more useful for pinpointing an exact moment in an experiment.
hints.easy: A specific indicator gives one clear, sudden color change right at a useful pH point, unlike the gradual rainbow of a universal indicator.

questions.text: In a chemical reaction, what determines the elements that can appear in the products?

options.text: The elements that were present in the reactants -- no new elements can be created in a normal chemical reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- chemical reactions only rearrange existing atoms into new combinations; they don't create or destroy elements.

options.text: Any element the chemist wants can simply appear in the products
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- ordinary chemical reactions can't introduce entirely new elements not already present in the reactants.

options.text: Products always contain completely different elements from the reactants
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- products are made of the SAME elements originally present in the reactants, just rearranged into new combinations.

options.text: Only reactions involving oxygen can determine product elements
options.feedback: This applies to all chemical reactions generally, not something unique to reactions specifically involving oxygen.

hints.hard: Chemical reactions rearrange existing atomic building blocks rather than creating entirely new ones.
hints.medium: A chemical reaction can only rearrange atoms that were already there to begin with.
hints.easy: A chemical reaction can only rearrange the atoms that were already there.

questions.text: If a reaction starts with only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms, why is it impossible for one of the products to contain nitrogen?

options.text: Chemical reactions cannot create new elements -- nitrogen atoms would have to already be present in the reactants for them to appear in a product
options.feedback: Correct -- this reflects the fundamental principle of conservation of elements/mass in chemical reactions.

options.text: Nitrogen atoms can spontaneously appear during any chemical reaction
options.feedback: This isn't possible under normal chemical reactions -- elements are conserved, not created, during typical chemistry.

options.text: This is actually possible and happens routinely in chemical reactions
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- ordinary chemical reactions cannot create entirely new elements not present among the original reactants.

options.text: Nitrogen is a special element that follows completely different rules
options.feedback: Nitrogen follows the same fundamental principle as every other element -- reactions can't create elements not already present in the reactants.

hints.hard: Consider the fundamental principle that chemical processes conserve the identity and quantity of every element present throughout the reaction.
hints.medium: Since nitrogen wasn't part of the starting materials, there's no way for it to just show up in the products.
hints.easy: Since nitrogen wasn't in the starting materials, it can't just show up in the products.

questions.text: Nuclear reactions, unlike ordinary chemical reactions, CAN actually transform one element into a different element entirely. Why does this fundamental distinction exist between chemical and nuclear processes?

options.text: Chemical reactions only involve rearranging electrons and bonds between atoms, while nuclear reactions involve changes within the atomic nucleus itself (protons/neutrons), which is what actually determines an element's identity
options.feedback: Correct -- since an element's identity is defined by its number of protons, only a nuclear-level change (unlike ordinary electron-based chemical bonding) can transform one element into another.

options.text: There is actually no real distinction between chemical and nuclear reactions
options.feedback: There is a very real, fundamental distinction -- chemical reactions involve electron rearrangement, while nuclear reactions involve changes to the nucleus itself, which is why only nuclear reactions can transmute elements.

options.text: Chemical reactions actually can transform elements just as easily as nuclear reactions
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- ordinary chemical reactions cannot change one element into another; that specifically requires a nuclear-level process.

options.text: Nuclear reactions don't actually involve atoms at all
options.feedback: Nuclear reactions definitely involve atoms -- specifically, changes occurring within their nuclei, which is the key distinguishing feature from ordinary chemical reactions.

hints.hard: An element's identity is defined specifically by its proton count, which chemical (electron-level) reactions cannot alter -- only nuclear-level processes affecting the proton count can transmute one element into another.
hints.medium: Chemical reactions only mess with the outer electrons, but changing what element something IS requires actually changing its nucleus, which only nuclear reactions can do.
hints.easy: Chemical reactions only mess with outer electrons, but changing what element something is requires changing its nucleus.

questions.text: If two samples both have the exact chemical formula H₂O and are pure, will they have the same physical properties (like boiling point)?

options.text: Yes, since they are chemically identical, their fundamental properties will be the same under the same conditions
options.feedback: Correct -- pure samples of the same compound share identical chemical and physical properties under matching conditions.

options.text: No, they will always have completely different properties
options.feedback: Pure samples of the exact same compound should have identical properties under the same conditions, not different ones.

options.text: It depends entirely on which country the water came from
options.feedback: Geographic origin doesn't affect the fundamental properties of a pure chemical compound -- its formula and structure do.

options.text: Properties are always completely random for any substance
options.feedback: Chemical and physical properties are actually determined by a substance's specific composition and structure, not randomness.

hints.hard: Chemically identical substances should exhibit identical characteristic behaviors under matching physical conditions.
hints.medium: Since they're the exact same pure substance, they should behave exactly the same way.
hints.easy: Since it's the exact same pure substance, it should act the same way every time.

questions.text: Why can chemists reliably predict a pure compound's properties (like melting point) just from knowing its identity, without needing to test every single sample?

options.text: A pure compound's properties are consistently determined by its fixed chemical composition and structure, which don't vary between different pure samples of the same substance
options.feedback: Correct -- this reliability and reproducibility of properties is a foundational principle that makes chemistry a predictive science.

options.text: Chemists actually cannot predict any compound's properties in advance
options.feedback: This isn't true -- chemists rely heavily on established properties of known pure compounds precisely because these properties are consistent and predictable.

options.text: Every single sample of a pure compound has completely different, unpredictable properties
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- properties of a pure compound are consistent and reproducible, not unpredictably variable between samples.

options.text: This predictability has nothing to do with chemical composition
options.feedback: This predictability is actually directly rooted in a compound's fixed, well-defined chemical composition and structure.

hints.hard: This predictability stems from the direct causal link between a compound's fixed molecular structure/bonding and its resulting physical/chemical behavior.
hints.medium: A pure compound's structure directly determines its properties, and that structure doesn't change from sample to sample.
hints.easy: A pure compound's structure stays the same, so its properties stay the same too.

questions.text: If a sample labeled as 'pure water' shows a boiling point significantly different from 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure, what would this most likely indicate?

options.text: The sample is likely not actually pure -- it probably contains dissolved impurities that are altering its boiling point
options.feedback: Correct -- deviations from a substance's known, expected properties are often used as practical evidence that a sample isn't as pure as claimed.

options.text: Water's boiling point actually varies randomly with no explanation
options.feedback: Water's boiling point at a given standard pressure is a well-established, consistent value -- an unexpected result more likely points to impurities or non-standard conditions.

options.text: The measurement definitely proves nothing unusual is happening
options.feedback: A significant deviation from the expected value for a supposedly pure substance IS a meaningful, notable finding worth investigating (likely impurities).

options.text: This result has no scientific significance at all
options.feedback: This kind of unexpected result actually has real scientific significance -- it's a practical, useful signal suggesting the sample may not be genuinely pure.

hints.hard: Established reference properties (like boiling point at standard pressure) serve as a diagnostic benchmark -- significant deviation strongly suggests the presence of contaminants altering the substance's expected behavior.
hints.medium: If something dissolved is mixed in with the water, it can change the boiling point away from the normal expected value.
hints.easy: If something else is mixed in with the water, it can change the boiling point away from normal.

questions.text: In the balanced equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, what is the mole ratio of hydrogen gas to oxygen gas used?

options.feedback: Correct -- the coefficients directly give the mole ratio: 2 moles of H₂ for every 1 mole of O₂.
This doesn't match the actual coefficients shown in the balanced equation.
This has the ratio backwards -- there are twice as many H₂ molecules as O₂ molecules, not the reverse.
This doesn't match the actual coefficients (2 for H₂, 1 for O₂) shown in the equation.

hints.hard: The numbers written directly in front of each substance's formula represent this ratio.
hints.medium: Look at the coefficients (the numbers in front of each formula) in the equation.
hints.easy: Look at the numbers in front of H₂ and O₂ in the equation -- 2 and 1.

questions.text: Using the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, if you have 6 moles of H₂ reacting completely, how many moles of O₂ are needed?

options.text: 3 moles
options.feedback: Correct -- using the 2:1 ratio, divide 6 by 2 to find the required O₂: 6÷2=3.

options.text: 6 moles
options.feedback: This ignores the 2:1 ratio, treating it as though it were 1:1.

options.text: 12 moles
options.feedback: This doubles instead of halving the hydrogen amount to find the oxygen needed.

options.text: 2 moles
options.feedback: This just repeats the coefficient value rather than correctly scaling it to match 6 moles of H₂.

hints.hard: Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to scale the known amount to find the corresponding required amount.
hints.medium: Since the ratio is 2:1, divide the hydrogen amount by 2 to find the oxygen needed.
hints.easy: Divide 6 by 2.

questions.text: Using the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, if 10 moles of H₂ react with 3 moles of O₂, which reactant is the limiting reactant, and how much water (in moles) is produced?

options.text: Oxygen is limiting; 6 moles of water are produced
options.feedback: Correct -- 3 moles of O₂ would need 6 moles of H₂ (2:1 ratio), but 10 are available, so oxygen runs out first, and 3 moles O₂ produces 2×3=6 moles of H₂O.

options.text: Hydrogen is limiting; 10 moles of water are produced
options.feedback: There's actually more than enough hydrogen available relative to the oxygen present -- oxygen is the one that runs out first.

options.text: Oxygen is limiting; 3 moles of water are produced
options.feedback: While oxygen is correctly identified as limiting, the water produced should be DOUBLE the oxygen amount (2:2 ratio in the equation), giving 6, not 3.

options.text: Neither reactant is limiting; both are used up completely
options.feedback: One reactant must run out first in this scenario -- checking the required ratio shows oxygen is the limiting reactant, with hydrogen left over.

hints.hard: Determine how much of one reactant would be needed to fully react with the given amount of the other, then compare against what's actually available to identify the limiting reactant and calculate the resulting product amount.
hints.medium: Figure out how much hydrogen would be needed to use up all 3 moles of oxygen, then compare that to the 10 moles available.
hints.easy: Check how much hydrogen 3 moles of oxygen would need (6), then compare to the 10 available -- oxygen runs out first.

questions.text: Compared to pure water, does salt water generally boil at a higher or lower temperature?

options.text: Higher
options.feedback: Correct -- dissolved salt raises the boiling point above that of pure water, a phenomenon called boiling point elevation.

options.text: Lower
options.feedback: This is backwards -- dissolved salt actually raises the boiling point, not lowers it.

options.text: Exactly the same temperature
options.feedback: Dissolved salt does have a measurable effect, raising the boiling point above that of pure water.

options.text: Salt water doesn't boil at all
options.feedback: Salt water absolutely can and does boil -- just at a slightly higher temperature than pure water.

hints.hard: Consider whether dissolving something in a liquid typically raises or lowers the temperature needed for it to boil.
hints.medium: Think about whether adding something dissolved usually makes it easier or harder for the liquid to boil.
hints.easy: Adding salt makes it a little harder for the water to boil, needing more heat.

questions.text: Why does adding salt to water raise its boiling point?

options.text: The dissolved salt particles interfere with water molecules escaping into vapor, requiring more energy (higher temperature) to reach boiling
options.feedback: Correct -- dissolved particles disrupt the process of water molecules leaving the liquid phase, requiring additional thermal energy to compensate.

options.text: Salt directly makes the water molecules move faster
options.feedback: The effect isn't about directly speeding up water molecules -- it's about the dissolved particles interfering with the vaporization process itself.

options.text: Salt has no actual effect on water's boiling point
options.feedback: Salt does have a measurable, real effect on boiling point, specifically raising it -- this is well-documented chemistry (boiling point elevation).

options.text: Salt actually cools the water down, which is why it takes longer to boil
options.feedback: The higher boiling point isn't due to net cooling -- it's due to the dissolved particles' interference with the phase-change (vaporization) process itself.

hints.hard: Dissolved particles occupy space at the liquid's surface, physically hindering the escape of solvent molecules into the vapor phase.
hints.medium: The dissolved salt particles get in the way of water molecules trying to escape into steam.
hints.easy: The dissolved salt particles get in the way of water molecules trying to turn into steam.

questions.text: Boiling point elevation depends on the NUMBER of dissolved particles, not necessarily their specific chemical identity. Why would adding the same molar amount of sugar versus salt to water have different effects on boiling point elevation?

options.text: Salt (like NaCl) dissociates into two separate ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) in water, effectively doubling the number of dissolved particles compared to the same molar amount of sugar, which doesn't dissociate at all
options.feedback: Correct -- since boiling point elevation depends on total particle count, salt's dissociation into two ions produces roughly double the effect of a non-dissociating solute like sugar at the same molarity.

options.text: Sugar and salt would have the exact same effect on boiling point, since they're added in the same molar amount
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- salt's ionic dissociation into two separate particles per formula unit gives it roughly double the boiling-point-elevating effect compared to sugar at the same molarity.

options.text: Sugar always has a stronger effect on boiling point than salt
options.feedback: This is backwards -- salt's dissociation into multiple ions typically gives it a STRONGER effect per mole than a non-dissociating solute like sugar.

options.text: This effect has nothing to do with the number of dissolved particles
options.feedback: This effect is actually directly and fundamentally tied to the total number of dissolved particles in solution, which is precisely why dissociation matters.

hints.hard: Boiling point elevation is a colligative property dependent on total solute particle concentration -- ionic compounds that dissociate into multiple ions per formula unit produce a proportionally larger effect than non-dissociating molecular solutes at equal molarity.
hints.medium: Salt splits apart into two separate charged pieces once dissolved, so it actually creates twice as many dissolved "things" as the same amount of sugar, which stays as one piece.
hints.easy: Salt splits into two separate pieces in water, so it creates twice as many dissolved bits as the same amount of sugar.

questions.text: Rusting of iron is an example of what type of chemical reaction?

options.text: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- rusting involves iron losing electrons (oxidizing) while oxygen gains them (reducing).

options.text: A neutralization reaction
options.feedback: Neutralization specifically involves an acid and a base reacting -- rusting is a different category (oxidation-reduction) of reaction.

options.text: A nuclear reaction
options.feedback: Rusting is an ordinary chemical process, not a nuclear reaction, which would involve changes to atomic nuclei.

options.text: No reaction occurs during rusting
options.feedback: Rusting is very much a real, observable chemical reaction between iron and oxygen (often with water present).

hints.hard: This reaction category is defined by simultaneous electron loss and electron gain between two participating substances.
hints.medium: This is the same broad category of reaction as electron transfer between substances.
hints.easy: This reaction involves iron and oxygen swapping electrons.

questions.text: Why does rusting typically happen faster in humid or wet environments compared to very dry ones?

options.text: Water acts as a medium that facilitates the electron transfer (redox) process between iron and oxygen, speeding up the reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- water helps ions move and interact more effectively, accelerating the overall rusting reaction.

options.text: Water actually prevents rusting from happening at all
options.feedback: This is backwards -- water generally SPEEDS UP rusting, rather than preventing it, by facilitating the necessary electron transfer process.

options.text: Humidity has no actual effect on the rusting process
options.feedback: Humidity does have a significant, well-documented effect on rusting rate, generally accelerating it.

options.text: Rusting only happens underwater, never in humid air
options.feedback: Rusting can happen in humid air (not just fully submerged underwater) -- moisture in the air is enough to facilitate and speed up the reaction.

hints.hard: Ionic movement and interaction, which drive electron transfer, are facilitated by the presence of a liquid medium like water.
hints.medium: Water helps the electrons and ions involved move around more easily, speeding up the whole process.
hints.easy: Water helps speed up the electron-swapping process that causes rust.

questions.text: Galvanized steel (steel coated with a layer of zinc) resists rusting even if the zinc coating gets scratched, exposing the steel underneath. Why does this protection persist even after the coating is damaged?

options.text: Zinc is more easily oxidized than iron, so the zinc will preferentially corrode (sacrificially) instead of the exposed iron, as long as some zinc remains in contact
options.feedback: Correct -- this 'sacrificial protection' strategy relies on zinc's greater tendency to oxidize, protecting the iron underneath even with some coating damage.

options.text: The scratch actually makes the zinc coating irrelevant, and rusting proceeds unaffected regardless
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- the remaining zinc coating continues to provide meaningful sacrificial protection even after a scratch, as long as it's still in electrical contact with the exposed steel.

options.text: Zinc is less reactive than iron, which is why it protects the steel
options.feedback: This is backwards -- zinc is actually MORE reactive (more easily oxidized) than iron, and this greater reactivity is exactly why it sacrificially protects the steel.

options.text: This protective effect has nothing to do with the relative reactivity of the two metals
options.feedback: This protective effect is actually directly and specifically explained by the relative reactivity difference between zinc and iron.

hints.hard: A more reactive metal (zinc) will preferentially undergo oxidation ahead of a less reactive one (iron) when both are exposed and electrically connected, providing ongoing protection to the iron as long as sacrificial zinc remains available.
hints.medium: Since zinc reacts more easily than iron, it 'takes the hit' and corrodes first, protecting the iron underneath even if the coating gets scratched.
hints.easy: Since zinc reacts more easily than iron, it corrodes first instead, protecting the iron underneath.

questions.text: What is electron shielding?

options.text: The effect where inner-shell electrons reduce the attractive pull of the nucleus on outer-shell electrons
options.feedback: Correct -- inner electrons partially block (shield) the nuclear charge from being fully felt by outer electrons.

options.text: A physical shield made of metal placed around an atom
options.feedback: This isn't a literal physical object -- it's an electronic effect involving how electrons interact with the nucleus's pull.

options.text: The process of an atom losing all its electrons
options.feedback: Electron shielding is about the interaction between existing electrons and the nucleus, not about losing electrons entirely.

options.text: A technique for protecting atoms from radioactivity
options.feedback: This isn't related to radiation protection -- it's specifically about how inner electrons affect the nuclear attraction felt by outer electrons.

hints.hard: This effect describes how electrons closer to the nucleus can partially block the nuclear pull experienced by more distant electrons.
hints.medium: This describes how inner electrons can partly block the nucleus's pull on outer electrons.
hints.easy: This is how inner electrons partly block the nucleus's pull on the outer ones.

questions.text: Why does atomic radius generally increase as you move down a group (column) on the periodic table?

options.text: Each additional electron shell increases both the distance from the nucleus and the shielding effect, both of which contribute to a larger atomic size
options.feedback: Correct -- adding new electron shells further from the nucleus, combined with increased shielding, results in progressively larger atoms down a group.

options.text: Atomic radius actually decreases as you move down a group
options.feedback: This is backwards -- atomic radius generally INCREASES moving down a group, due to additional electron shells.

options.text: Electron shielding has no effect on atomic radius
options.feedback: Electron shielding is actually a significant contributing factor to the trend of increasing atomic radius down a group.

options.text: Atoms lower in a group have fewer protons than atoms higher up
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- atomic number (proton count) actually INCREASES moving down a group, not decreases.

hints.hard: Consider how the addition of an entirely new, farther-out electron shell affects both distance from the nucleus and the cumulative shielding provided by all inner shells.
hints.medium: Each new row down means an entirely new outer shell, which is both farther away and gets more shielding from the shells beneath it.
hints.easy: Each new row down means a whole new outer shell, farther from the nucleus.

questions.text: Moving ACROSS a period (row) on the periodic table (left to right), atomic radius generally DECREASES, even though more protons and electrons are being added. Why doesn't increased electron shielding prevent this shrinking trend across a period?

options.text: Within the same period, new electrons are added to the SAME outer shell rather than a new one, so shielding doesn't increase proportionally, while nuclear charge (protons) does increase, pulling electrons in more tightly
options.feedback: Correct -- since electrons are added to the same energy level, the increasing nuclear charge dominates over the relatively unchanged shielding, resulting in a smaller atomic radius.

options.text: Electron shielding actually increases dramatically across a period, more than compensating for the added protons
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- shielding stays relatively constant within the same shell across a period, which is exactly why the increasing nuclear charge can dominate and shrink the atom.

options.text: Atoms across a period all have the exact same number of protons
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- proton count (atomic number) increases by one with each step across a period, which is central to explaining the shrinking radius trend.

options.text: This trend has no real explanation in atomic theory
options.feedback: This is actually a well-understood, well-explained trend rooted in the relationship between nuclear charge and electron shielding within the same shell.

hints.hard: Since additional electrons within the same period occupy the same principal energy level, the shielding contribution remains relatively constant, allowing the steadily increasing nuclear charge to progressively pull the electron cloud inward.
hints.medium: Since the new electrons are going into the same outer shell (not a new one), they don't shield each other much better, but the growing pull from more protons wins out.
hints.easy: Since the new electrons stay in the same outer shell, they don't block much extra, so the growing pull from more protons wins out.

questions.text: What is the general purpose of a titration in chemistry?

options.text: To determine the unknown concentration of a solution by reacting it with a solution of known concentration
options.feedback: Correct -- titration uses a precisely measured reaction to calculate an unknown concentration.

options.text: To measure the temperature of a solution
options.feedback: Temperature measurement isn't the primary purpose of titration -- it's specifically for determining concentration.

options.text: To change the color of a solution permanently
options.feedback: While titrations often use color-changing indicators, the actual PURPOSE is determining concentration, not just changing color.

options.text: To create a new element
options.feedback: Titration is an analytical technique for concentration determination, not a method for creating new elements.

hints.hard: This technique uses a precisely controlled reaction to work backward and calculate an unknown quantity.
hints.medium: This process uses a known solution to help figure out an unknown solution's strength.
hints.easy: This process figures out how strong an unknown solution is by reacting it with a known one.

questions.text: During an acid-base titration, what does the 'endpoint' (often signaled by an indicator's color change) represent?

options.text: The point at which the acid and base have reacted in stoichiometrically equivalent amounts
options.feedback: Correct -- this endpoint approximates the true equivalence point, providing the data needed to calculate the unknown concentration.

options.text: The point at which the experiment must be completely restarted
options.feedback: The endpoint isn't a restart signal -- it's the crucial measurement point used to calculate the unknown concentration.

options.text: The moment the solution reaches its boiling point
options.feedback: The endpoint relates to the chemical reaction reaching stoichiometric completion, not a temperature-related boiling event.

options.text: The point where all the color disappears completely and permanently
options.feedback: The endpoint is defined by a specific color CHANGE (often to a new color), not necessarily a total absence of color.

hints.hard: This is the observed signal (often a color change) used to approximate the true stoichiometric equivalence point of the reaction.
hints.medium: This is the moment the indicator changes color, signaling the reaction has reached the right proportions.
hints.easy: This is when the indicator changes color, showing the reaction is basically complete.

This just repeats the base's concentration, without correctly accounting for the different volumes used.
