hints.easy: This mountain range runs along the western edge of South America.

questions._topic: the Chavin culture of the Andes

questions.text: Chavin artwork is especially known for stylized carvings of which powerful animal, believed to hold deep religious significance?

options.text: The jaguar
options.feedback: Correct -- feline imagery, especially jaguar-like faces and fangs, pervades Chavin stone carvings and iconography.

options.text: The eagle alone
options.feedback: Raptor imagery does appear in Chavin art, but its most emphasized and recognizable motif is the feline, not the eagle alone.

options.text: The horse
options.feedback: Horses were not present in the Americas until Europeans introduced them much later -- they play no role in Chavin imagery.

options.text: The elephant
options.feedback: Elephants never existed in South America, so they have no place in Chavin religious art.

hints.hard: This predator's stylized face and fangs recur throughout Chavin religious art, distinct from bird or livestock imagery from Old World cultures.
hints.medium: This big cat's fanged, snarling face appears repeatedly in Chavin stone carvings.
hints.easy: This animal is a large, powerful cat known for its strength and stealth.

questions._topic: the Chavin culture of the Andes

questions.text: Because Chavin's distinctive religious iconography and artistic style spread widely across the Andes without evidence of military conquest, archaeologists often describe it as what kind of culture?

options.text: A 'horizon' culture, spread mainly through shared religion, art, and trade rather than conquest
options.feedback: Correct -- the 'Chavin Horizon' describes how its influence spread through belief and exchange rather than warfare.

options.text: A military empire that conquered its neighbors, similar to the later Inca
options.feedback: Unlike the Inca, Chavin's influence is not attributed to military conquest -- it spread through shared religious and artistic ideas.

options.text: A maritime empire built on overseas colonization
options.feedback: Chavin's influence spread across the Andean highlands and coast through trade and belief, not overseas colonization.

options.text: A nomadic confederation without any fixed ceremonial centers
options.feedback: Chavin was centered on a major fixed temple complex at Chavin de Huantar, not a nomadic society.

hints.hard: This term distinguishes cultural and religious diffusion across a wide region from empire-building through military campaigns, overseas colonies, or nomadic wandering.
hints.medium: This term describes influence spreading through religion and trade, not soldiers and conquest.
hints.easy: Think about how ideas can spread through shared belief and trade instead of armies.

questions._topic: the Chavin culture of the Andes

questions.text: Angkor Wat, one of the largest religious monuments in the world, is located in which present-day country?

options.text: Cambodia
options.feedback: Correct -- Angkor Wat sits near Siem Reap in modern Cambodia, once the heart of the Khmer Empire.

options.text: Thailand
options.feedback: Thailand borders the region but Angkor Wat itself lies within modern Cambodia.

options.text: Vietnam
options.feedback: Vietnam lies to the east of Cambodia and was not home to the Khmer capital of Angkor.

options.text: Indonesia
options.feedback: Indonesia is a separate archipelago nation, not the location of Angkor Wat.

hints.hard: This country's name is closely tied to the Khmer people who built the great temple complex near modern Siem Reap.
hints.medium: This country lies between Thailand and Vietnam in mainland Southeast Asia.
hints.easy: This Southeast Asian country is home to the ancient Angkor temple complex.

questions._topic: Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire

questions.text: Angkor Wat was originally built as a temple dedicated to which Hindu god, before gradually becoming a Buddhist site over the centuries?

options.text: Vishnu
options.feedback: Correct -- Angkor Wat was originally consecrated as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu.

options.text: Shiva
options.feedback: Many earlier Khmer temples honored Shiva, but Angkor Wat itself was dedicated to Vishnu.

options.text: Brahma
options.feedback: Brahma was not the deity Angkor Wat was consecrated to -- that was Vishnu.

options.text: Ganesha
options.feedback: Ganesha is a widely worshipped Hindu god, but Angkor Wat's dedication was specifically to Vishnu.

hints.hard: This deity, not Shiva or Brahma, was the one Angkor Wat's builders chose to honor in its original dedication.
hints.medium: This deity is part of the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Shiva.
hints.easy: This god is one of the principal deities of Hinduism, often depicted with four arms.

questions._topic: Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire

questions.text: Which Khmer king commissioned the construction of Angkor Wat in the early 12th century?

options.text: Suryavarman II
options.feedback: Correct -- Suryavarman II commissioned Angkor Wat as his state temple and likely mausoleum in the early 1100s.

options.text: Jayavarman VII
options.feedback: Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom and the Bayon temple decades later -- Angkor Wat itself was Suryavarman II's project.

options.text: Jayavarman II
options.feedback: Jayavarman II is credited with founding the Khmer Empire centuries earlier, not with building Angkor Wat.

options.text: Indravarman I
options.feedback: Indravarman I ruled much earlier and built other Khmer monuments, not Angkor Wat.

hints.hard: This king, distinct from the founder of the Khmer Empire and from the later builder of Angkor Thom and the Bayon, is credited specifically with Angkor Wat itself.
hints.medium: This king ruled in the early 1100s, before the later ruler who built Angkor Thom.
hints.easy: This king's name begins with a word meaning 'sun' in Sanskrit -- a prefix none of the other three rulers listed share.

questions._topic: Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire

questions.text: The Srivijaya Empire was a powerful maritime trading empire based on which Indonesian island?

options.text: Sumatra
options.feedback: Correct -- Srivijaya was centered near modern Palembang on the island of Sumatra.

options.text: Java
options.feedback: Java was later home to the Majapahit Empire, not the earlier Srivijaya, which was based on Sumatra.

options.text: Borneo
options.feedback: Borneo was not the seat of Srivijaya's power -- that was the island of Sumatra.

options.text: Bali
options.feedback: Bali is a much smaller island and was not the center of the Srivijaya Empire.

hints.hard: This island's coastal city of Palembang was the seat of a maritime trading power that controlled nearby shipping lanes.
hints.medium: This large island lies west of Java in the Indonesian archipelago.
hints.easy: This island is home to the modern Indonesian city of Palembang.

questions.text: Srivijaya's control over which strategic waterway made it central to trade between India and China?

options.text: The Strait of Malacca
options.feedback: Correct -- controlling this narrow, busy passage let Srivijaya tax and profit from ships moving between India and China.

options.text: The Strait of Hormuz
options.feedback: The Strait of Hormuz is near the Persian Gulf, far from Srivijaya's Southeast Asian territory.

options.text: The Bosphorus
options.feedback: The Bosphorus links the Black Sea and Mediterranean near Constantinople, unrelated to Southeast Asian trade routes.

options.text: The Sunda Strait
options.feedback: The Sunda Strait lies further south between Sumatra and Java, but it was the Strait of Malacca that defined Srivijaya's dominance.

hints.hard: This narrow, heavily trafficked passage between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra -- not a strait near the Middle East or Europe -- was Srivijaya's economic lifeline.
hints.medium: This waterway was the key shipping lane linking Indian Ocean and South China Sea trade.
hints.easy: This narrow passage lies between the Malay Peninsula and the island of Sumatra.

questions.text: A famous Chinese Buddhist monk traveled to Srivijaya in the 7th century to study Buddhist scriptures there and later wrote an account of the empire. Who was this monk?

options.text: Yijing (I-Tsing)
options.feedback: Correct -- Yijing studied at Srivijaya's Buddhist centers of learning and documented the empire in his writings.

options.text: Xuanzang
options.feedback: Xuanzang famously traveled overland to India to study Buddhism, not to Srivijaya by sea.

options.text: Faxian
options.feedback: Faxian traveled to India generations earlier and is not the monk associated with studying in Srivijaya.

options.text: Zheng He
options.feedback: Zheng He was a Ming Dynasty admiral centuries later, not a Buddhist scholar-monk studying in Srivijaya.

hints.hard: This monk, distinct from the famous overland traveler to India and from a much later Ming naval admiral, documented his years of study at Srivijaya's Buddhist institutions.
hints.medium: This monk's journey and studies took him through Srivijaya on his way to and from India.
hints.easy: This monk traveled by sea and spent years studying Buddhism in Southeast Asia.

questions.text: The Majapahit Empire, one of the last major Hindu-Buddhist empires of Southeast Asia, was centered on which island?

options.text: Java
options.feedback: Correct -- Majapahit's capital and heartland were on the island of Java.

options.text: Sumatra
options.feedback: Sumatra was home to the earlier Srivijaya Empire, not Majapahit's core territory.

options.text: Borneo
options.feedback: Borneo was not the center of Majapahit power -- that was the island of Java.

options.text: Sulawesi
options.feedback: Sulawesi lies further east and was not Majapahit's core territory.

hints.hard: This island, distinct from Sumatra's earlier maritime power, was the heartland of a later empire that reached its peak in the 14th century.
hints.medium: This island lies east of Sumatra and was the heartland of a later, different empire than Srivijaya.
hints.easy: This island is also home to Indonesia's modern capital region and largest population.

questions.text: Majapahit reached its greatest extent and influence during the reign of which king, working alongside his powerful chief minister Gajah Mada?

options.text: Hayam Wuruk
options.feedback: Correct -- under Hayam Wuruk and Gajah Mada, Majapahit's influence stretched across much of maritime Southeast Asia.

options.text: Raden Wijaya
options.feedback: Raden Wijaya founded Majapahit generations earlier -- its peak came later, under Hayam Wuruk.

options.text: Kertanegara
options.feedback: Kertanegara ruled the earlier Singhasari kingdom, which predated Majapahit.

options.text: Suryavarman II
options.feedback: Suryavarman II was a Khmer king who built Angkor Wat, unrelated to Majapahit in Java.

hints.hard: This king, not the empire's founder nor an earlier rival kingdom's ruler, presided over Majapahit's widest territorial reach alongside his chief minister.
hints.medium: This king reigned during Majapahit's golden age, well after its founding.
hints.easy: This ruler worked alongside a famous chief minister who swore to unify the archipelago.

questions.text: Because Majapahit's sphere of influence once stretched across much of the modern Indonesian archipelago and beyond, the empire is often invoked in modern Indonesia as what?

options.text: A historical symbol of territorial unity for the modern Indonesian nation
options.feedback: Correct -- Majapahit's wide reach is frequently cited as a precedent for Indonesia's modern national boundaries and identity.

options.text: Evidence of early Islamic governance in the region
options.feedback: Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist empire -- widespread Islamic governance in the archipelago came later, after Majapahit's decline.

options.text: The origin of Indonesia's modern parliamentary system
options.feedback: Indonesia's parliamentary system is a 20th-century development, unrelated to Majapahit's governance structure.

options.text: The source of the Indonesian language's grammar
options.feedback: Modern Indonesian is based on Malay, not directly derived from Majapahit-era Javanese governance.

hints.hard: This role concerns how a sprawling pre-colonial empire's reach is used today as a symbolic precedent, distinct from religious, linguistic, or governmental claims.
hints.medium: This role is about national symbolism and unity, not religion, government structure, or language.
hints.easy: Think about how a powerful, far-reaching ancient kingdom might be remembered by a much later nation.

questions.text: Which of the following are true about the Byzantine Empire? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was the continuation of the Roman Empire's eastern half
options.feedback: Correct -- after Rome's western half fell, its eastern half continued on as the Byzantine Empire.

options.text: Its capital was Constantinople
options.feedback: Correct -- Constantinople served as the Byzantine Empire's capital for over a thousand years.

options.text: It was founded by Charlemagne
options.feedback: Charlemagne founded the later Carolingian Empire in Western Europe -- he did not found the Byzantine Empire.

options.text: It fell in 476 CE, the same year as the Western Roman Empire
options.feedback: 476 CE only marks the Western Roman Empire's fall -- the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire survived for nearly another thousand years, until 1453.

hints.hard: Think broadly about this empire's deep historical roots and the general part of the world where its power was centered, rather than any single ruler's name or an unrelated continent.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve Rome's legacy and a city straddling Europe and Asia.
hints.easy: One correct answer is about which older empire this one continued from; the other is about its famous capital city.

questions.text: Which of the following accurately describe the Byzantine Empire's institutions and culture? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It preserved and continued Roman legal and administrative traditions
options.feedback: Correct -- Byzantine emperors maintained and adapted Roman law and bureaucracy for centuries.

options.text: Its dominant religion, after its early centuries, was Eastern Orthodox Christianity
options.feedback: Correct -- the Byzantine Empire became a center of Eastern Orthodox Christian practice and theology.

options.text: It abandoned Roman legal traditions in favor of an entirely unrelated legal system
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire didn't discard Roman law -- it preserved and adapted Roman legal and administrative traditions for centuries.

options.text: It was governed by an elected parliament with no monarch
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire was ruled by emperors, not by an elected parliamentary system.

hints.hard: Think broadly about which institutions carried over from the past and which faith became dominant, rather than any claim about discarding the old system entirely or ruling without a monarch.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve carrying forward Roman traditions and adopting a particular branch of Christianity.
hints.easy: One correct answer is about law and government; the other is about religion.

questions.text: Which of the following accurately distinguish the Byzantine Empire from the Western Roman Empire that collapsed in 476 CE? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It survived for roughly another thousand years after Rome's western half fell
options.feedback: Correct -- the Byzantine Empire endured until 1453, nearly a millennium after the west's collapse.

options.text: Its dominant language gradually shifted from Latin to Greek
options.feedback: Correct -- over time, Greek became the empire's primary administrative and cultural language.

options.text: It was conquered by the Visigoths in the 5th century
options.feedback: The Visigoths were involved in the Western Roman Empire's fall, not the Byzantine (eastern) empire's downfall.

options.text: It never faced any external military threats until 1453
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire faced centuries of invasions and wars long before its final fall in 1453.

hints.hard: Think broadly about how this empire's lifespan and everyday culture set it apart from its western counterpart, rather than any single invading group or how often conflict arose.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve the empire's long survival and a linguistic shift, not who conquered the west or how peaceful its history was.
hints.easy: One correct answer is about how long it lasted; the other is about its main language changing over time.

questions.text: Byzantine Emperor Justinian I is best known for commissioning a comprehensive compilation of Roman law known as what?

options.text: The Justinian Code (Corpus Juris Civilis)
options.feedback: Correct -- Justinian ordered scholars to compile and organize centuries of Roman law into this influential code.

options.text: The Twelve Tables
options.feedback: The Twelve Tables were an much earlier Roman law code, from the early Roman Republic, not Justinian's compilation.

options.text: The Edict of Milan
options.feedback: The Edict of Milan was Emperor Constantine's earlier decree on religious tolerance, not a legal code.

options.text: The Nicene Creed
options.feedback: The Nicene Creed is a statement of Christian religious belief, not a body of civil law.

hints.hard: This achievement organized and preserved a vast body of existing law under one ruler's direction -- think about the general type of large-scale intellectual project this represents, rather than any specific era or document name.
hints.medium: This is a body of law, distinct from earlier Roman codes or unrelated religious and imperial edicts.
hints.easy: This achievement is a massive legal compilation, not a building or a military campaign.

questions.text: Justinian's military campaigns, led by his general Belisarius, were primarily aimed at achieving what overarching goal?

options.text: Reconquering the lost western territories of the former Roman Empire
options.feedback: Correct -- Justinian sought to restore Roman rule over regions like Italy and North Africa that had fallen to other powers.

options.text: Converting the empire's population to Islam
options.feedback: Islam did not yet exist during Justinian's reign in the 6th century -- his goal was western reconquest.

options.text: Establishing new trade colonies in China
options.feedback: Justinian's campaigns focused on Mediterranean territories, not establishing colonies in East Asia.

options.text: Conquering the entirety of the Persian Empire
options.feedback: Justinian fought costly wars with Persia but his primary strategic goal was reclaiming the lost Roman west.

hints.hard: Think about the general type of ambition this represents -- looking backward to restore something once held, rather than looking outward to gain something entirely new.
hints.medium: This goal involved reclaiming lands the empire had already once ruled, in the west.
hints.easy: Think about restoring old territory rather than gaining brand-new lands far away.

questions.text: Justinian's legal code was organized into several parts; which part was specifically intended as an introductory textbook for law students?

options.text: The Institutes
options.feedback: Correct -- the Institutes summarized legal principles in a form designed for teaching students.

options.text: The Digest (Pandects)
options.feedback: The Digest was a large compilation of earlier jurists' legal opinions, not the student textbook portion.

options.text: The Codex
options.feedback: The Codex compiled imperial laws and decrees, not the introductory teaching text.

options.text: The Novellae
options.feedback: The Novellae collected new laws issued after the main code was completed, not the student textbook.

hints.hard: Think about which audience this particular part of the code was written for, and what kind of document serves that audience, rather than the specific alternative parts by name.
hints.medium: This part was a simplified summary for teaching, distinct from the larger scholarly compilations.
hints.easy: This part was meant for students just learning the law, not practicing judges.

questions.text: The Hagia Sophia, famous for its massive dome, was originally built as what type of structure?

options.text: A Christian cathedral
options.feedback: Correct -- the Hagia Sophia was built as a grand Byzantine Christian cathedral in Constantinople.

options.text: A mosque
options.feedback: It was later converted into a mosque after the Ottoman conquest, but it was originally built as a Christian cathedral.

options.text: A Roman bathhouse
options.feedback: It was never built as a bathhouse -- its original purpose was as a grand Christian cathedral.

options.text: A royal palace
options.feedback: It served a religious, not residential, purpose from the start, as a Christian cathedral.

hints.hard: This building's original religious use came before it was later converted to serve a different faith following a conquest; it was not a secular structure like a bathhouse or a palace.
hints.medium: This building served as the seat of the Byzantine church's central cathedral.
hints.easy: This structure's original purpose was religious worship for Christians.

questions.text: The Hagia Sophia was commissioned by which Byzantine emperor and completed in the 6th century?

options.text: Justinian I
options.feedback: Correct -- Justinian I had the Hagia Sophia built, completing it in 537 CE.

options.text: Constantine the Great
options.feedback: Constantine founded Constantinople two centuries earlier, but Justinian I commissioned the Hagia Sophia itself.

options.text: Theodosius II
options.feedback: Theodosius II built an earlier cathedral on the site, but the grand structure standing today was Justinian's project.

options.text: Basil II
options.feedback: Basil II ruled centuries after the Hagia Sophia's construction, not the emperor who commissioned it.

hints.hard: This emperor, distinct from the founder of Constantinople two centuries earlier and from a much later ruler, is the one credited with completing the standing structure in 537 CE.
hints.medium: This emperor reigned in the 6th century and rebuilt this structure after riots damaged an earlier version.
hints.easy: This emperor also commissioned a famous compilation of Roman law.

questions.text: After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453, the Hagia Sophia was converted into what, before later becoming a museum in the 20th century?

options.text: A mosque
options.feedback: Correct -- the Ottomans converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque, adding minarets and Islamic religious features.

options.text: A fortress
options.feedback: It retained a religious function under Ottoman rule as a mosque, rather than becoming a military fortress.

options.text: A marketplace
options.feedback: The building continued to serve a religious purpose as a mosque, not a commercial marketplace.

options.text: A library
options.feedback: It functioned as a place of worship, a mosque, rather than a library, following the Ottoman conquest.

hints.hard: This new function, under Ottoman rule, was religious in nature -- distinct from a defensive fortress, a commercial marketplace, or a repository of books.
hints.medium: Minarets were added to the building for this new religious purpose.
hints.easy: This new use was religious, tied to the faith of the conquering empire.

questions.text: Which of the following were among the first four caliphs of the Rashidun Caliphate, who led the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad's death? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Abu Bakr
options.feedback: Correct -- Abu Bakr became the first Rashidun caliph after Muhammad's death in 632 CE.

options.text: Umar ibn al-Khattab
options.feedback: Correct -- Umar was the second Rashidun caliph, overseeing major early conquests.

options.text: Suleiman the Magnificent
options.feedback: Suleiman was an Ottoman sultan who ruled nearly a thousand years later, not one of the Rashidun caliphs.

options.text: Saladin
options.feedback: Saladin was a much later Ayyubid sultan famous for opposing the Crusaders, not a Rashidun caliph.

hints.hard: Both correct answers belong to the earliest generation of Muslim leaders, distinct from a much later Ottoman sultan and a later Ayyubid sultan famous for the Crusades era.
hints.medium: Both correct answers ruled in the 7th century, right after Muhammad's death, not centuries later.
hints.easy: One correct answer is the very first leader after Muhammad; the other led major conquests as the second leader.

questions._topic: the Rashidun Caliphate and early Islamic expansion

questions.text: Which of the following are true about the Rashidun Caliphate's early military conquests? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It rapidly expanded beyond the Arabian Peninsula into former Byzantine and Persian territory
options.feedback: Correct -- within decades, Rashidun armies conquered vast lands once held by Byzantium and Persia.

options.text: It brought about the total collapse of the Sassanid Persian Empire
options.feedback: Correct -- the Sassanid Empire was completely overrun and ended by Rashidun conquests.

options.text: It never expanded beyond the Arabian Peninsula
options.feedback: The Rashidun Caliphate expanded dramatically beyond Arabia, into the Levant, Egypt, and Persia.

options.text: It was primarily a naval empire with little land expansion
options.feedback: The Rashidun conquests were driven primarily by land armies, not naval power.

hints.hard: One correct answer is about how far the conquests reached; the other is about a Persian empire's fate.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve conquest beyond Arabia and the end of a major Persian dynasty.
hints.easy: Both correct statements describe expansion into former Byzantine and Persian lands and the complete downfall of a specific Persian dynasty, not a claim of staying confined to Arabia or of relying mainly on naval power.

questions._topic: the Rashidun Caliphate and early Islamic expansion

questions.text: Which of the following accurately describe the Rashidun Caliphate specifically, as distinct from the later Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Its caliphs succeeded one another through selection among early companions of Muhammad, rather than hereditary dynastic succession
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike the later hereditary caliphates, the Rashidun caliphs were chosen from among Muhammad's early companions.

options.text: It ended with the assassination of Ali and the rise of the Umayyad dynasty
options.feedback: Correct -- Ali's assassination in 661 CE marked the Rashidun era's end and the start of Umayyad rule.

options.text: It moved its capital permanently to Baghdad
options.feedback: Baghdad was founded and became a capital under the later Abbasid Caliphate, not the Rashidun era.

options.text: It was ruled by a hereditary dynasty founded by Muawiyah
options.feedback: Muawiyah founded the hereditary Umayyad dynasty after the Rashidun period ended, not during it.

hints.hard: One correct answer is about how leaders were chosen; the other is about how this era ended.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve a non-hereditary succession method and a violent transition to the next caliphate.
hints.easy: Both correct statements concern a selection-based (not hereditary) leadership method and the violent end of this era, distinct from a later capital city and a later hereditary dynasty's founding.

questions._topic: the Rashidun Caliphate and early Islamic expansion

questions.text: The Umayyad Caliphate, one of the largest empires in history, established its capital in which city?

options.text: Damascus
options.feedback: Correct -- the Umayyads made Damascus their capital, ruling a vast empire from this Syrian city.

options.text: Baghdad
options.feedback: Baghdad became the capital under the later Abbasid Caliphate, not the Umayyads.

options.text: Cairo
options.feedback: Cairo rose to prominence under later Islamic dynasties, not as the Umayyad capital.

options.text: Mecca
options.feedback: Mecca remained Islam's holiest city, but the Umayyad seat of political power was Damascus.

hints.hard: This Syrian city, not the later Abbasid capital or Islam's holiest city, was where the Umayyads ruled their vast empire.
hints.medium: This city was the political heart of the Umayyad dynasty, distinct from the later Abbasid capital.
hints.easy: This city is in modern Syria and gives its name to a well-known style of early Islamic mosque architecture.

questions.text: The Umayyad Caliphate's territory stretched from the Iberian Peninsula in the west to which region in the east?

options.text: The Indus River valley
options.feedback: Correct -- Umayyad territory reached as far east as the Indus valley in present-day Pakistan.

options.text: The eastern coast of China
options.feedback: Umayyad rule never extended to China's coast -- its eastern edge reached the Indus valley.

options.text: The coast of Japan
options.feedback: Japan was far beyond Umayyad reach -- its eastern border was the Indus valley.

options.text: Australia
options.feedback: Australia was entirely unconnected to the Umayyad world -- its territory extended only as far as the Indus valley in the east.

hints.hard: This river valley, not a coastal region of China, Japan, or Australia, marked the eastern limit of Umayyad territorial reach.
hints.medium: This region marks the far eastern edge of Umayyad expansion, in South Asia.
hints.easy: This river flows through present-day Pakistan.

questions.text: After being overthrown by the Abbasid Revolution in 750 CE, a surviving Umayyad prince fled westward and founded a new Umayyad state in which region?

options.text: Al-Andalus (Iberia/Spain)
options.feedback: Correct -- Abd al-Rahman I escaped to Iberia and established the Emirate of Cordoba, continuing Umayyad rule there.

options.text: Persia
options.feedback: Persia became the heartland of the new Abbasid Caliphate, not a refuge for the fleeing Umayyad prince.

options.text: Egypt
options.feedback: The surviving Umayyad prince passed through parts of North Africa but ultimately established his new state in Iberia, not Egypt.

options.text: Anatolia
options.feedback: Anatolia was largely Byzantine territory at the time, not where the exiled Umayyad prince founded his new state.

hints.hard: This region, distinct from the new Abbasid heartland in Persia, from Egypt, and from Byzantine Anatolia, became the refuge where Umayyad rule continued for centuries more.
hints.medium: This region became home to a new Umayyad emirate centered at Cordoba.
hints.easy: This region is in southwestern Europe, once home to a long-lasting Islamic state.

questions.text: The Abbasid Caliphate, which overthrew the Umayyads in 750 CE, established its new capital in which city?

options.text: Baghdad
options.feedback: Correct -- the Abbasids built Baghdad as their new capital, which became a major center of learning and trade.

options.text: Damascus
options.feedback: Damascus had been the Umayyad capital -- the Abbasids moved the seat of power to Baghdad instead.

options.text: Cairo
options.feedback: Cairo rose to prominence under other later dynasties, not as the Abbasid capital.

options.text: Medina
options.feedback: Medina was significant in early Islamic history, but the Abbasid capital was Baghdad.

hints.hard: This city rose along a major Mesopotamian river under the dynasty that seized power in a mid-8th-century revolution, later becoming renowned for its intellectual life.
hints.medium: This city became a major Abbasid center of trade and scholarship, distinct from the earlier Umayyad capital.
hints.easy: This city sits along the Tigris River in modern Iraq.

questions._topic: the Abbasid Caliphate and the House of Wisdom

questions.text: The House of Wisdom, a major intellectual center in Baghdad, was especially known for what activity that preserved and expanded classical knowledge?

options.text: Translating Greek, Persian, and Indian scholarly texts into Arabic
options.feedback: Correct -- scholars at the House of Wisdom translated and built upon works from many earlier civilizations.

options.text: Printing the first books using movable type
options.feedback: Movable-type printing in this form developed elsewhere and much later -- the House of Wisdom's core activity was translation and scholarship.

options.text: Minting the very first coins in history
options.feedback: Coinage predates the House of Wisdom by many centuries -- its defining activity was translation and scholarly research.

options.text: Building the first observatories anywhere in the world
options.feedback: Observatories existed in earlier civilizations too -- the House of Wisdom's central legacy was its translation movement.

hints.hard: This activity bridged the learning of earlier, distant civilizations into the Arabic-speaking world, rather than any single invention sometimes wrongly credited to this era.
hints.medium: Scholars here worked to bring older works, written in other languages, into wider Arabic circulation.
hints.easy: This activity involved converting texts from one language into Arabic.

questions._topic: the Abbasid Caliphate and the House of Wisdom

questions.text: The House of Wisdom is credited with reaching its greatest prominence as a formal institution under the patronage of which Abbasid caliph in the early 9th century?

options.text: Al-Ma'mun
options.feedback: Correct -- al-Ma'mun is widely credited with formally establishing and expanding the House of Wisdom as a major center of scholarship.

options.text: Al-Mansur
options.feedback: Al-Mansur founded Baghdad itself decades earlier, but the House of Wisdom's peak is credited to al-Ma'mun.

options.text: Al-Mutawakkil

questions.text: The Reconquista refers to the centuries-long effort by Christian kingdoms to retake control of which peninsula from Muslim rule?

options.text: The Byzantine Empire

options.text: The Holy Roman Empire
options.feedback: The Holy Roman Empire, part of the defending coalition, continued on for over a century after this battle.

options.text: The Hanseatic League
options.feedback: The Hanseatic League's decline stemmed from separate economic shifts, unrelated to the 1683 battle.

hints.hard: This decline affected the empire on the attacking side of the siege, distinct from an empire that had already fallen over two centuries earlier, the defending empire itself, or an unrelated trading alliance.
hints.medium: This turning point affected the empire that had been besieging the city, not the defenders.
hints.easy: Think about which side's momentum began reversing after this battle.

questions.text: The dramatic climax of the 1683 Battle of Vienna is often attributed to a massive cavalry charge carried out by which distinctive Polish cavalry force?

options.text: The winged hussars
options.feedback: Correct -- the winged hussars' charge, led by Sobieski, is often described as one of the largest cavalry charges in history and helped break the siege.

options.text: The Ottoman Janissaries
options.feedback: The Janissaries were elite Ottoman infantry on the besieging side, not the Polish cavalry that charged to relieve the city.

options.text: The Teutonic Knights
options.feedback: The Teutonic Knights were a medieval military order from an earlier era, not the force credited with this 1683 charge.

options.text: The Cossack Host
options.feedback: Cossack forces existed and fought in this era, but the decisive charge at Vienna is specifically credited to the Polish winged hussars.

hints.hard: This cavalry force, serving Poland and distinct from the besieging army's elite infantry, an earlier medieval military order, or a separate irregular cavalry force, delivered the battle's decisive charge.
hints.medium: This cavalry force served the Polish king and charged downhill to break the siege.
hints.easy: This cavalry force is famous for distinctive decorative wings attached to their armor.

questions.text: Marco Polo, a Venetian merchant traveler, journeyed across Asia in the 13th century to reach the court of which powerful ruler?

options.text: Kublai Khan
options.feedback: Correct -- Marco Polo traveled to the court of Kublai Khan, the Mongol ruler of Yuan Dynasty China.

options.text: Genghis Khan
options.feedback: Genghis Khan, Kublai's grandfather, had died decades before Marco Polo's journey -- it was Kublai Khan whose court Polo visited.

options.text: Tamerlane
options.feedback: Tamerlane built his empire generations after Marco Polo's travels, not the ruler Polo visited.

options.text: Suleiman the Magnificent
options.feedback: Suleiman ruled the Ottoman Empire centuries after Marco Polo's travels.

hints.hard: This ruler, distinct from his own more famous grandfather, from a much later Central Asian conqueror, and from a later Ottoman sultan, presided over the court Marco Polo visited.
hints.medium: This ruler founded a Mongol dynasty that governed a vast East Asian empire.
hints.easy: This ruler was a grandson of a more famous earlier Mongol conqueror.

questions.text: Marco Polo's famous written account of his travels was dictated to a fellow writer while Polo was held where?

options.text: As a prisoner of war in Genoa
options.feedback: Correct -- Polo dictated his account to a writer named Rustichello da Pisa while both were imprisoned in Genoa.

options.text: In a monastery in Venice
options.feedback: Polo was not in a monastery when he dictated his account -- he was imprisoned in Genoa after a naval battle.

options.text: At the Mongol court itself
options.feedback: The written account was produced after Polo's return to Europe, while he was imprisoned, not while still at the Mongol court.

options.text: Aboard a ship en route home
options.feedback: The dictation happened during his imprisonment in Genoa, after his voyage home, not during the voyage itself.

hints.hard: This place, distinct from a religious retreat, the distant Mongol court, or a ship headed home, is where Polo was being held after his capture in a sea battle between two rival Italian maritime powers.
hints.medium: This was a period of captivity following a naval conflict between Italian city-states.
hints.easy: This place is a city in Italy, not Asia.

questions.text: Marco Polo's account describes years of service in Kublai Khan's court, within a Mongol-led dynasty that ruled which country?

options.text: China (the Yuan Dynasty)
options.feedback: Correct -- Kublai Khan founded the Yuan Dynasty, ruling China, where Polo claimed to have served in various capacities.

options.text: Persia (the Ilkhanate)
options.feedback: The Ilkhanate was a separate Mongol khanate ruling Persia -- Polo's account centers on Kublai Khan's rule over China.

options.text: Russia (the Golden Horde)
options.feedback: The Golden Horde was a separate Mongol khanate ruling over Russian lands, distinct from Kublai Khan's rule over China.

options.text: India (the Mughal Empire)
options.feedback: The Mughal Empire was founded centuries after Marco Polo's travels and ruled India, not China.

hints.hard: This country was governed by a dynasty founded by the same Mongol khan whose court Polo entered, setting it apart from Mongol-controlled lands farther west.
hints.medium: This country's ruling dynasty at the time was founded by the very khan Polo served.
hints.easy: This country is in East Asia and was ruled by a Mongol-founded dynasty during Polo's travels.

questions.text: The Mali Empire's ruler Mansa Musa is famous in history for being considered what, largely due to his kingdom's vast gold resources?

options.text: Possibly the richest person in history
options.feedback: Correct -- Mansa Musa's immense wealth, built on West African gold and salt trade, has led many historians to call him the richest person in recorded history.

options.text: The first Muslim ruler in Africa
options.feedback: Muslim rulers existed in parts of Africa well before Mansa Musa -- his fame rests on his extraordinary wealth, not being the first.

options.text: The founder of the Songhai Empire
options.feedback: The Songhai Empire was a separate, later West African power -- Mansa Musa ruled Mali, not Songhai.

options.text: The last pharaoh of Egypt
options.feedback: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire in West Africa, entirely unrelated to Egypt's pharaohs.

hints.hard: This reputation, distinct from claims about being first in religion, founding a different empire, or Egyptian rulership, rests specifically on the sheer scale of his kingdom's gold wealth.
hints.medium: This reputation comes from control of gold and salt trade routes across West Africa.
hints.easy: This reputation is about wealth, not military conquest or religious leadership.

questions._topic: the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa

questions.text: Mansa Musa's fame in the wider medieval world grew largely from his lavish pilgrimage in 1324 to which holy city?

options.text: Mecca
options.feedback: Correct -- Mansa Musa's hajj to Mecca, accompanied by an enormous retinue and vast quantities of gold, became legendary.

options.text: Jerusalem
options.feedback: Jerusalem was not the destination of Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage -- his hajj was to Mecca.

options.text: Rome
options.feedback: Rome was not the destination of this pilgrimage -- Mansa Musa's journey was an Islamic hajj to Mecca.

options.text: Timbuktu
options.feedback: Timbuktu was part of Mansa Musa's own empire and a stop that grew from his journey's fame, not the pilgrimage's destination.

hints.hard: This city, the destination of the Islamic hajj, is distinct from a Christian holy city, the seat of the Roman Catholic Church, or Mansa Musa's own empire's famous trading city.
hints.medium: This city is in the Arabian Peninsula and is the goal of the hajj.
hints.easy: This city is Islam's holiest destination for pilgrimage.

questions._topic: the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa

questions.text: Mansa Musa's hajj famously caused a temporary economic disruption in which city, where his massive gold spending caused the value of gold to crash for years afterward?

options.text: Cairo
options.feedback: Correct -- Mansa Musa's lavish gold spending while passing through Cairo reportedly devalued gold in the regional economy for years.

options.text: Baghdad
options.feedback: The economic disruption occurred in Cairo, along Mansa Musa's pilgrimage route, not in Baghdad.

options.text: Constantinople
options.feedback: Constantinople was not on Mansa Musa's hajj route -- the gold-driven economic disruption happened in Cairo.

options.text: Timbuktu
options.feedback: Timbuktu was Mansa Musa's own empire's city, not the foreign city where his spending disrupted gold prices.

hints.hard: This Egyptian city, distinct from a Mesopotamian capital, a Byzantine capital, or Mansa Musa's own West African capital, is where his spending famously crashed gold values.
hints.medium: This city's gold market reportedly took years to recover after Mansa Musa passed through.
hints.easy: This city is in Egypt, along the route of Mansa Musa's journey.

questions._topic: the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa

questions.text: The Songhai Empire rose to become the dominant power in West Africa after the decline of which earlier empire?

options.text: The Mali Empire
options.feedback: Correct -- Songhai grew into the region's dominant power as the once-mighty Mali Empire weakened.

options.text: The Ottoman Empire
options.feedback: The Ottoman Empire was based far to the north and east, not the West African power Songhai succeeded.

options.text: The Kingdom of Aksum
options.feedback: Aksum was an East African kingdom, not the West African power whose decline allowed Songhai's rise.

options.text: The Byzantine Empire
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire was based in southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, unrelated to West African Songhai's rise.

hints.hard: Think about which major West African empire held power across the region before Songhai's rise, and what caused that empire to give way to a new dominant force.
hints.medium: This earlier empire dominated West African trade routes for centuries before its decline opened the way for Songhai.
hints.easy: This empire was once ruled by a famously wealthy king remembered for a legendary pilgrimage to Mecca.

questions.text: Songhai's capital and major trade hub, sitting along the Niger River, was which city?

options.text: Gao
options.feedback: Correct -- Gao served as the Songhai Empire's political capital along the Niger River.

options.text: Marrakesh
options.feedback: Marrakesh was a major city in Morocco, not the Songhai Empire's capital.

options.text: Cairo
options.feedback: Cairo was Egypt's great city, far from Songhai's core territory along the Niger River.

options.text: Fez
options.feedback: Fez was another major Moroccan city, not Songhai's capital.

hints.hard: This city lies along a major West African river.
hints.medium: This city was Songhai's political center, an important hub of trade and governance.
hints.easy: This city, situated on the Niger River, served as the seat of Songhai's imperial power.

questions.text: The Songhai Empire's power was ultimately broken in 1591 by an invading Moroccan army that succeeded largely due to its use of what technology, giving it a decisive advantage over Songhai's forces?

options.text: Firearms (gunpowder muskets)
options.feedback: Correct -- Moroccan forces armed with muskets and cannons overwhelmed Songhai's largely traditional army at the Battle of Tondibi.

options.text: Cavalry alone
options.feedback: Songhai itself fielded strong cavalry forces -- the decisive Moroccan advantage came from gunpowder weapons, not cavalry.

options.text: Naval warships
options.feedback: This was an inland conflict fought far from any coast -- naval power played no role in Songhai's defeat.

options.text: Siege towers
options.feedback: Medieval-style siege towers were not the deciding factor -- it was gunpowder firearms that overwhelmed Songhai's forces.

hints.hard: Think about what kind of relatively new weaponry might have given the smaller invading army a decisive edge over Songhai's traditional forces.
hints.medium: This technology relied on gunpowder to fire projectiles, offering a major advantage over more traditional arms.
hints.easy: This technology involved gunpowder weapons like muskets and cannons, giving the invading force a decisive military edge.

questions.text: Which of the following were East African Swahili Coast trading city-states? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Kilwa
options.feedback: Correct -- Kilwa was a wealthy Swahili Coast trading city-state on the East African coast.

options.text: Mombasa
options.feedback: Correct -- Mombasa was another major Swahili Coast trading city-state.

options.text: Timbuktu
options.feedback: Timbuktu was an inland West African center of trade and scholarship, not a Swahili Coast city-state on the Indian Ocean.

options.text: Gao
options.feedback: Gao was the capital of the Songhai Empire in West Africa, not an East African Swahili Coast city-state.

hints.hard: Both correct answers are coastal East African cities, not inland West African ones.
hints.medium: Both true answers sit along the Indian Ocean coastline, not along West Africa's Niger River region.
hints.easy: Both correct answers are Indian Ocean coastal trading cities, distinct from the inland West African centers of Timbuktu and Gao.

questions.text: Which of the following are true about the Swahili Coast city-states? (Select all that apply)

options.text: They grew wealthy primarily through trade across the Indian Ocean
options.feedback: Correct -- Swahili Coast cities thrived by connecting African goods with Arab, Persian, and Indian Ocean trade networks.

options.text: Their culture and language blended Bantu African traditions with Arab, Persian, and Indian influences
options.feedback: Correct -- Swahili culture and language reflect centuries of this Indian Ocean cultural blending.

options.text: They were united under a single centralized empire ruled from one capital
options.feedback: The Swahili Coast was made up of independent, competing city-states, not a single unified empire.

options.text: They had no contact with traders from outside East Africa
options.feedback: Extensive Indian Ocean trade contact with Arabia, Persia, and India was central to these city-states' wealth and culture.

hints.hard: One correct answer is about which ocean brought wealth; the other is about cultural blending.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve maritime trade connections and a mixed cultural heritage, not isolation or centralized rule.
hints.easy: Both correct statements describe Indian Ocean trade wealth and a blended Bantu-Arab-Persian-Indian culture, distinct from claims of full political unification or total isolation.

questions.text: Which of the following accurately describe Kilwa's role among the Swahili Coast city-states? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It became especially wealthy by controlling access to gold exported from the inland kingdom of Great Zimbabwe
options.feedback: Correct -- Kilwa's control of this gold trade route made it one of the richest Swahili Coast city-states.

options.text: It minted its own coins, reflecting its wealth and commercial sophistication
options.feedback: Correct -- Kilwa's minting of coins is notable evidence of its economic power among Swahili Coast city-states.

options.text: It was the political capital of a single unified Swahili empire ruling the whole coast
options.feedback: Kilwa was a powerful independent city-state, but the Swahili Coast was never unified under one capital or empire.

options.text: It was located far inland, away from the Indian Ocean coastline
options.feedback: Kilwa was a coastal port city -- its wealth depended directly on Indian Ocean maritime trade access.

hints.hard: One correct answer is about gold from an inland kingdom; the other is about coinage.
hints.medium: Both true statements involve Kilwa's specific economic achievements, not a claim about ruling the whole coast.
hints.easy: Both correct statements describe Kilwa's specific gold-trade wealth and its own minted currency, distinct from an inaccurate claim of unifying the coast or being located away from the sea.

questions.text: The eleven medieval churches at Lalibela, Ethiopia, are famous for being constructed how, distinguishing them from most other churches?

options.text: Carved directly downward out of solid rock
options.feedback: Correct -- the Lalibela churches were monolithically carved out of volcanic rock, rather than built upward from stone blocks.

options.text: Assembled entirely from imported marble blocks
options.feedback: The churches were carved from the existing bedrock, not assembled from imported marble.

options.text: Built to float on a nearby lake
options.feedback: The churches are fixed structures carved into solid ground, not floating structures.

options.text: Constructed entirely from wood
options.feedback: The churches are famous specifically for being carved from solid rock, not built from wood.

hints.hard: This method involved subtraction rather than addition -- removing stone rather than stacking it.
hints.medium: This method meant the churches are literally part of the volcanic bedrock itself.
hints.easy: This method, carving downward into solid volcanic rock rather than building with imported stone, wood, or floating construction, makes these churches structurally unique.

questions._topic: the Ethiopian Empire and the rock churches of Lalibela

questions.text: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela were commissioned under which Ethiopian king, for whom the town is named?

options.text: King Lalibela (Gebre Mesqel Lalibela)
options.feedback: Correct -- King Lalibela commissioned these remarkable churches, and the town later took his name.

options.text: Emperor Haile Selassie
options.feedback: Haile Selassie was a 20th-century Ethiopian emperor, far later than the medieval king who commissioned the Lalibela churches.

options.text: King Ezana
options.feedback: King Ezana ruled the earlier Kingdom of Aksum in the 4th century, well before Lalibela's churches were built.

options.text: Menelik II
options.feedback: Menelik II ruled Ethiopia in the 19th and early 20th centuries, long after the Lalibela churches were carved.

hints.hard: This king's name is now also the name of the town itself.
hints.medium: This king ruled in the medieval period, centuries before Ethiopia's 19th- and 20th-century rulers.
hints.easy: This king, distinct from a much later 20th-century emperor, an earlier 4th-century Aksumite king, and a later 19th-century emperor, is the namesake of the town and its churches.

questions._topic: the Ethiopian Empire and the rock churches of Lalibela

questions.text: Ethiopia's Christian tradition, one of the oldest in the world, traces its formal adoption as a state religion to the 4th-century reign of which Aksumite king?

options.text: King Ezana
options.feedback: Correct -- King Ezana of Aksum adopted Christianity as the kingdom's official religion in the 4th century.

options.text: King Lalibela
options.feedback: King Lalibela ruled centuries later, in the 12th and 13th centuries, after Christianity was already long established in Ethiopia.

options.text: Emperor Haile Selassie
options.feedback: Haile Selassie ruled in the 20th century, over a millennium after Christianity's formal adoption under Ezana.

options.text: Menelik I
options.feedback: Menelik I is a legendary founding figure of the Solomonic dynasty, not the historical king credited with adopting Christianity.

hints.hard: This king ruled many centuries before the churches of Lalibela were carved.
hints.medium: This king ruled the earlier Kingdom of Aksum, before the later Solomonic dynasty era.
hints.easy: This king, ruling Aksum in the 4th century and distinct from the later Lalibela, Haile Selassie, or the legendary Menelik I, is credited with Christianity's formal adoption.
